slides.text: nums = [2, 4, 1, 5, 3]. What's the sum from index 1 to 3? 4 + 1 + 5 = 10.
slides.alt: The array nums, 2, 4, 1, 5, 3, indexed 0 to 4, with a bracket over indices 1 to 3 labelled 4 + 1 + 5 = 10.

slides.text: Any trip = end reading − start reading. You never re-drive the trip.
slides.alt: "An odometer: total distance since the car was new." Trip start 12,040 km, trip end 12,075 km, so the trip = 12,075 − 12,040 = 35 km.

slides.text: A prefix array is that odometer: 0, 2, 6, 7, 12, 15.
slides.alt: nums 2, 4, 1, 5, 3 above its prefix array, the running total: 0, 2, 6, 7, 12, 15.

slides.text: Then, for each x, the next slot is the previous slot plus x.
slides.alt: Python build_prefix(nums): prefix = [0] * (len(nums) + 1); for i, x in enumerate(nums): prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + x, with the loop highlighted, and range_sum returning prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l]. The note reads "Next slot = previous slot + x"; the stage fills prefix[4] = 7 + 5 = 12.

slides.text: 1..3 → 12 − 2 = 10. 2..4 → 15 − 6 = 9. One subtraction, however wide the range.
slides.alt: nums with indices 1 to 3 bracketed, and the prefix array 0, 2, 6, 7, 12, 15 with 2 and 12 ringed: 12 − 2 = 10.

slides.text: Our test run, 10,000 queries on 100,000 numbers (Python): 4.96 s summing each range vs 6.1 ms with a prefix array, build included.
slides.alt: "10,000 queries on 100,000 numbers, our test run, Python": sum(nums[l:r+1]) each time takes 4.96 s; the prefix array, build included, takes 6.1 ms. A tag says about 800× faster.

slides.text: Off-by-one: prefix[r] − prefix[l] drops nums[r] (7 − 2 = 5, not 10).
slides.alt: "The classic off-by-one": prefix[r] - prefix[l] gives sum(1..3) → 7 − 2 = 5 ✗, which drops the last number, nums[3] = 5; prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l] gives 10 ✓.
